claims.subject: Grafting
claims.text: For a graft to succeed, the vascular tissues must grow together.

references.label: P1.1
references.text: Grafting or graftage[1] is a horticultural technique whereby tissues of plants are joined so as to continue their growth together.

references.label: P1.2
references.text: The upper part of the combined plant is called the scion (/ˈsaɪən/) while the lower part is called the rootstock.

references.label: P1.3
references.text: The success of this joining requires that the vascular tissues grow together.

references.label: P1.4
references.text: The natural equivalent of this process is inosculation.

references.label: P1.5
references.text: The technique is most commonly used in asexual propagation of commercially-grown plants for the horticultural and agricultural trades.

references.label: P1.6
references.text: The scion is typically joined to the rootstock at the soil line; however, top-work grafting may occur far above this line, leaving an understock consisting of the lower part of the trunk and the root system.

claims.subject: Pruning
claims.text: A reason for pruning unwanted material is to limit the potential for pathogen intrusion and decay.

references.label: P5.1
references.text: The practice entails the targeted removal of diseased, damaged, dead, non-productive, structurally unsound, or otherwise unwanted plant material from crop and landscape plants.

references.label: P5.2
references.text: In general, the smaller the branch that is cut, the easier it is for a woody plant to compartmentalize the wound and thus limit the potential for pathogen intrusion and decay.

references.label: P5.3
references.text: It is therefore preferable to make any necessary formative structural pruning cuts to young plants, rather than removing large, poorly placed branches from mature plants.
